text:
Maya (People Ops): quick Q from a new parent planning leave across a move: they want parental leave to start on the day their partner travels to another state for delivery. payroll asked if we can shift the official leave start date for tax/residency reasons. can folks weigh in?
Ravi: do we have a policy about aligning leave start with delivery events vs. when the employee actually stops working?
Maya (People Ops): policy: leave start date is the first calendar day the employee is off work for parental reasons. we can record an administrative 'anticipated start' for planning, but payroll/benefits follow the actual leave start for deductions and taxes.
Lina: scenario: employee currently lives in CA, partner gives birth in OR and family plans to stay in OR for 10 days. do we need to change payroll state for that short period?
Tax Bot: short answer: generally no. Payroll state stays with your primary work/state of record unless the employee changes residency or does extended remote work. Short travel for medical events doesn't trigger state tax changes. Exceptions if the employee changes payroll address on record.
Alex (Manager): manager perspective: we want benefits (health premiums, stipend) to continue uninterrupted and not force the employee into a new benefits enrollment. is that OK?
Payroll Bot: benefits continue as long as employee remains on payroll enrollment. If you take unpaid leave and deductions stop, benefits may lapse. For short paid leave, nothing changes. If you plan unpaid leave that spans payroll cutoffs, submit the leave and benefits checklist at least 2 payroll cycles prior.
Ravi: and what about local paid family leave (PFL) filings? employee might file CA PFL if employer is CA-based and they meet requirements, but if the child is born in another state, is that still fine?
Tax Bot: PFL eligibility is based on the employee's work/state and their contribution history to the state's program. Birth location doesn't change eligibility. For CA PFL, the employee must meet wage and contribution thresholds; People Ops can help with the claim paperwork.
Maya (People Ops): practical steps for the employee: 1) pick the calendar date they will stop working (official leave start). 2) tell manager + People Ops so we can log the leave and run benefit impact. 3) if traveling out-of-state for delivery, keep People Ops posted if you'll extend remote work beyond 30 days (we'll check tax/residency).
Lina: is there a preferred phrasing the manager should use when approving an anticipated start to keep records straight?
Maya (People Ops): manager can email People Ops with: "Approve anticipated leave start <date> pending delivery. Employee will notify People Ops within 24hrs of actual stop date." we'll create an anticipated entry but will only trigger payroll changes on actual leave start.
Alex (Manager): got it. i'll approve that phrasing and tell the IC.
Maya (People Ops): last note: if employee wants reimbursements (travel-related childcare, pump rental while traveling), submit receipts and tag expense as "Lactation & Family Supplies" or "Parental Travel" and cc People Ops for pre-approval. finance will need dates and proof of medical appointment if required.
Payroll Bot: Reminder: to avoid benefit gaps, submit leave paperwork 2 payroll cycles before planned unpaid deductions stop: https://intranet.redwood/leave/submit
Maya (People Ops): thanks all  i'll DM the employee and add the guidance to the leave packet so managers can copy the approval snippet.
Ravi: thanks  for the clarity.
